target_customer: Schools and teachers (and originally teens and parents) teaching creative JavaScript coding to grades 3 to 12
problem: Block coding tools do not lead teens to real programming and few resources engage girls and underrepresented students.
business_model: School and district subscriptions for a coding curriculum platform

founders.name: Alexandra Diracles
founders.background_notes: Met co-founders at a 2014 Startup Weekend hackathon per TechCrunch. A search result lists her as an NYU alumna, not verified from an opened page.

founders.name: Leandra Tejedor
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by TechCrunch and Learning.com; not listed on the YC page.

competitors.name: Scratch
competitors.what: MIT block based visual programming and sharing site that Vidcode positions itself as the step after

technical_complexity.rationale: Browser based coding lessons with video and image filter libraries; standard web engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Curriculum content and school adoption gave some stickiness, but many comparable platforms existed.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: None bought it; a smaller coding company, Codesters, acquired Vidcode in 2021.

market_need_then: TechCrunch in July 2017 reported over 25,000 schools using Vidcode and Arkansas schools using it to meet a state coding requirement, showing demand tied to coding mandates.

identity.voice_and_tone: Teen oriented, built around Snapchat filters, memes and videos

branding.brand_signature: Snapchat geofilter coding contest that drew over 10,000 entries in 2016
branding.community_and_virality: 2016 geofilter contest with over 10,000 entries and TechCrunch and EdSurge coverage.

brand_strength.rationale: The name states what it does and the geofilter contest and school adoption gave visibility, but the brand ended as a product inside an acquirer.

pivots.from: Teens and parents coding with Snapchat filters and videos
pivots.why: Not stated; the current site describes a K-12 school and library curriculum

outcome_analysis: Vidcode began as a 2014 Startup Weekend project, joined YC in Summer 2016, raised a 1.5M dollar seed in July 2017 and reached over 25,000 schools by then. It stayed small, with no later round found, and was acquired by Codesters in 2021, which Learning.com bought in January 2023. The exit looks like a modest consolidation in K-12 edtech; price is undisclosed.
notes: A 100K dollar Intel Capital investment in 2015 appears in one search summary only, so it is unverified and not a round. The YC blog was seen only in search results for the Scratch positioning. Learning.com post dateline conflicts (2022 versus 2023). Vidcode site fetch showed only navigation. No funding after 2017 found; Wellfound and CB Insights show 1.5M latest.
